isw.title: Every basin models ISW numerically — but not every model estimates depletion
isw.body: All six subbasins characterize interconnected surface water with a numerical groundwater–surface water model, the approach the literature calls the gold standard. What the models report differs. Merced and Salinas Valley isolate pumping-attributable depletion by running the model with and without pumping, and Kaweah — whose model is not yet calibrated for streams — substitutes an analytical depletion function. East Turlock, Colusa and Yolo report net stream–aquifer exchange from all causes and call it depletion, and Colusa and Yolo describe their ISW results as provisional or uncalibrated on most streams.

isw.title: Groundwater levels stand in for modeled depletion
isw.body: No basin uses model output as its ISW compliance measure. Five test compliance on groundwater elevations at near-stream wells, and Salinas Valley, Colusa and Yolo cite EDF (2018) for that proxy. The plans give their reasons: models not calibrated to individual streams, uncertainty too large to quantify depletion reliably, and — in Salinas Valley — the judgment that annual model updates are unrealistic. Merced shows how the proxy is defended: a scenario at its thresholds added 38,000 AFY of depletion, about 1.6% of surface outflow, which the GSP judged small enough for groundwater levels to protect streams.

isw.title: Thresholds and undesirable results are defined on groundwater levels
isw.body: Five of the six basins set ISW criteria on groundwater elevations — Merced by carrying over its chronic-lowering thresholds rather than setting ISW-specific ones. What counts as an undesirable result varies widely: any one shallow well in Salinas Valley, half of a river's wells for two consecutive falls in East Turlock, the same three of twelve wells for 24 months in Colusa, and more than half the wells in two or more management zones in Yolo. Kaweah has not defined a basin-wide undesirable result; its self-described "placeholder" criteria set one flow threshold, on one reach of the Lower Kaweah River.

isw.title: Depletion volumes are not tied to thresholds — or always to pumping
isw.body: Where a basin publishes a depletion volume, it neither sets nor tests a threshold. Merced estimates 504,400 AFY of pumping-attributable depletion and uses none of it in its criteria. Salinas Valley's 2020 volumetric threshold of 69,700 AF/yr was net exchange from all causes; a later no-pumping run put pumping's share at 8,400 AF/yr, and Amendment 1 replaced the volume with a groundwater-level proxy. East Turlock's annual "depletion" totals — including a 28,700 AF net gain on the San Joaquin — come from no with-and-without-pumping comparison, so none is attributed to pumping.

isw.title: Monitoring networks differ in size and depth, and grow on grants
isw.body: The wells behind the groundwater-level proxy vary widely. Salinas Valley's ISW network ran on one usable well for its entire evaluation period, after a second proved to be screened beneath the aquitard; Colusa uses 12 near-stream wells under 200 feet deep and Yolo 17 shallow wells across five zones, while East Turlock's shallow network includes wells screened hundreds of feet below the water table. Depth matters because pumping is often deeper: in Salinas Valley essentially all of it is below the aquitard, a link to the river no study has yet measured. New ISW wells and gages are mostly grant-funded, and Colusa and Yolo list remedies without dates or funding.

isw.title: "Significant and unreasonable" is mostly anchored to the last drought
isw.body: SGMA leaves the definition of significant and unreasonable depletion to each GSA, and most reach for a recent drought: Fall 2015 groundwater levels in East Turlock and Colusa (plus 10 feet of "operational flexibility" in Colusa), and 2015 levels plus one foot in Salinas Valley. Kaweah is the exception in kind, anchoring to streamflow rather than groundwater — low flows below WY 2022 levels on one reach. Yolo sets its Upper Sacramento thresholds 63–65 feet below its objectives to allow for expected cuts in surface-water deliveries. The literature points to an ecological alternative: flow criteria set from habitat needs, as in the California Environmental Flows Framework.

isw.title: Uncertainty in depletion estimates is rarely quantified
isw.body: The literature treats reporting uncertainty alongside a depletion estimate as essential. Kaweah is the one basin to do so numerically: its 1.4 cfs estimate for the Lower Kaweah carries a 90% likelihood range from 100,000 Monte Carlo runs, and it publishes model calibration statistics. Colusa labels its ISW conclusions provisional and the other basins describe uncertainty in prose; none bounds a depletion volume. Merced's 2026 Rules add a numeric uncertainty buffer — but to the groundwater-level trigger, not to depletion.

mlrp.title: Repurposing runs through several programs, each answering to a different agency
mlrp.body: Four subbasins hold Department of Conservation MLRP block grants of $8.89–10 million, but the grantee varies: a GSA in Merced, the subbasin in East Turlock and Kaweah, and a regional non-GSA water management group in Salinas Valley. Alongside them run GSA programs — Merced's fee-funded Phase 1 Land Repurposing Program, which had repurposed 14,128 acres by WY 2025, and East Turlock's three-year Incentivized Fallowing Program — and Kaweah also took part in DWR's LandFlex, which idled land near at-risk domestic wells. In every basin the activity that idles the most land sits outside MLRP, so program results reach the groundwater accounting by different routes, if at all.

mlrp.title: Repurposing goals are set in acre-feet, in acres, or not at all
mlrp.body: Merced commits to 25,911 AF of savings over five years and measured about 4,655 AF in WY 2025 — roughly 10% short on an annual basis. East Turlock targets 21,000 acres, 3,880 more than its own suitability analysis could locate; the difference is a "Miscellaneous Repurposing" placeholder carrying 19% of the headline water benefit. Kaweah's MLRP targets are acres only — about 238 acres of recharge basins and 65 or more of habitat — with no water figure, and Salinas Valley's repurposing action names a benefit type with no quantity.

mlrp.title: Water savings are calculated after implementation, before it, or not at all
mlrp.body: Merced measures savings after implementation, parcel by parcel, with OpenET through its accounting platform — and found reductions lower than expected because orchard trees and wet-year soil moisture kept transpiring. East Turlock estimates savings once, beforehand (2.7 AF per acre from satellite ET, revised to 2.9 with its groundwater model three months later), and exempts enrolled parcels from ET measurement. Kaweah computes no savings figure: a fallowed field simply stops being debited, and its three GSAs each treat fallow land differently. The literature finds the ET-minus-precipitation method least reliable on exactly the transitioning land these programs create.

mlrp.title: Benefits beyond water are named and scored, but rarely measured
mlrp.body: Every grantee basin names ecological, community and economic benefits, and none measures a delivered outcome for them inside its repurposing program. Merced scores benefits at application on a points rubric with no published formula; East Turlock prices them — rewilding pays $410 per acre per year more than extended fallowing for an identical water obligation, which makes that difference the price of habitat. Salinas Valley holds the most rigorous ecological method in the study, an annually repeatable vegetation threshold for groundwater-dependent ecosystems, but it is unadopted and measures groundwater depth rather than repurposing.

mlrp.title: Each basin decides differently where a repurposed parcel's allocation goes
mlrp.body: In Merced, enrolled landowners choose whether to give up their allocation; most keep it, and because idled land is neither debited nor reduced, the allocation accumulates and can be carried over or transferred. East Turlock rescinds the allocation of paid parcels for the agreement term, so a landowner cannot be paid not to pump and keep the right to pump. Kaweah leaves the allocation portable, even between GSAs, but scales a transfer leave-behind by distance and has run pilot market auctions. Salinas Valley has no allocation system yet; it buys or leases the land, removing the pumper rather than regulating them.

mlrp.title: Parcels are chosen top-down by suitability analysis or bottom-up by landowner interest
mlrp.body: East Turlock sited its program with an auditable suitability analysis — named stream buffers and slope thresholds over public datasets, ground-truthed with aerial imagery — and Salinas Valley is building a recharge-suitability and multi-criteria decision tool with UC Davis. MKGSA uses Sustainable Conservation's Groundwater Recharge Assessment Tool to pursue parcels for acquisition, though its plan declares the tool advisory. Merced instead relies on landowner applications, scored on a rubric whose formula and award threshold are unpublished; in Colusa and Yolo, repurposing-type projects are proposed and run mostly by partners such as The Nature Conservancy, districts and community groups.

community.title: Domestic-well impacts are not reported by community
community.body: The literature finds that domestic wells inside disadvantaged communities are less likely than wells elsewhere to be protected by local minimum thresholds, and that thousands of domestic and public supply wells could still go dry even if current sustainability criteria are met. Some basins estimate domestic-well exposure — Colusa counts wells above candidate thresholds — but in Colusa about half of the underlying well records lack screen depth, and many locations are approximate.

community.title: Help arrives after the well fails
community.body: Most dry-well programs reviewed provide support after a household loses water. MKGSA plans to notify well owners as conditions approach levels that could affect their wells. Those notices depend on a voluntary well registry; the GSAs expect some owners to hesitate over privacy and property values, and plan to build trust through communication with local communities. Eligibility for support also depends on linking a well problem to groundwater management.

community.title: Community benefit has no unit
community.body: Turlock's GSP records community benefit within MLRP management actions as an overlap with benefits to sustainability indicators, while also naming recreation and public health. Yolo uses yes-or-no flags in its proposed management actions table to identify projects that benefit disadvantaged communities. The documents define no unit for these fields, so benefits are not yet tracked or compared across projects, and it is not yet clear whether a link between community benefit and groundwater accounting is feasible.

community.title: A board seat is not decision authority
community.body: The literature finds that formal board representation predicts equity-related plan content better than outreach does. Plans describe who holds board seats and which committees advise the boards, and Yolo specifically describes the seats tied to disadvantaged communities. The plans say less about how seats and voting rules shape accounting decisions such as fees and pumping limits. In Salinas Valley, those two decisions require a supermajority that includes three of four agricultural representatives.

community.title: Language access is uneven
community.body: Turlock introduced Spanish-language access for video-based SGMA communication, fact sheets, and flyers promoting the Water Leadership Institute in partnership with EDF, and offered translation on request for Technical Advisory Committee meetings. MKGSA's mitigation plan includes a stakeholder outreach plan with at least one workshop in an underrepresented community, in English and Spanish.

community.title: Water-quality thresholds cover few constituents
community.body: Basins differ in which constituents carry water-quality thresholds. Merced focuses solely on salinity, Colusa on electrical conductivity, and Turlock on total dissolved solids. Salinas Valley reports constituents that exceed a regulatory standard, relying on the State's Title 22 drinking-water standards. Constituents requested by commenters, such as PFAS, were not adopted for lack of historical data and drinking-water standards. In East Turlock, expanded domestic-well testing runs through the State Water Board's SAFER program.

community.title: Accounting platforms are built for growers
community.body: Research on decision-driven data systems finds that different users need data in different formats, and stresses engaging decision stakeholders who may not have deep technical expertise; other work shows community knowledge can fill data gaps and build capacity for local policy decisions. The accounting platforms reviewed are built for landowners and growers. Community-facing products appear separately, such as Kaweah's seasonal groundwater-quality report and Salinas Valley's story map. Many community-facing resources exist — the Drinking Water Tool, CalEnviroScreen — but the plans do not yet point residents to them. In Salinas, the Castroville Community Services District is quoted asking for more outreach and education, specifically about seawater intrusion.
